generic: Sodium Acid Phosphate (Sodium Phosphate Monobasic; Sodium Dihydrogen Phosphate)
cls: Urinary acidifier / phosphorus (phosphate) replacement supplement; component of oral saline laxatives and bowel preparations
pharm: Acidic sodium salt of phosphoric acid (monosodium dihydrogen phosphate), often combined with disodium (dibasic) phosphate. Provides phosphate for replacement of body phosphorus, acidifies the urine, and - in osmotic saline laxative/bowel-prep forms - draws water into the bowel lumen.
tags: FDA boxed warning on oral sodium phosphate bowel preps (acute phosphate nephropathy)
quick: Urinary acidification: 250 mg orally 4 times daily (max 2,000 mg/day); phosphate replacement dosed in mmol per serum phosphorus
Take oral phosphate with or after food and a full glass of water to reduce GI upset
Generally low risk when used appropriately; correct deficiency as needed
Caution - reduce/avoid; risk of hyperphosphatemia and acute phosphate nephropathy
No direct interaction; alcohol may worsen dehydration with laxative use
Serum phosphorus, calcium, sodium, potassium, renal function; urine pH for acidification
summary: Sodium acid phosphate (sodium phosphate monobasic / sodium dihydrogen phosphate), frequently combined with the dibasic (disodium) salt, is used for three main purposes: (1) urinary acidification (to lower urine pH, reduce urinary odor, and support certain stone/infection management), (2) phosphorus (phosphate) replacement in hypophosphatemia or as a phosphate supplement, and (3) as the active component of saline (osmotic) laxatives and oral bowel-cleansing preparations before colonoscopy. For urinary acidification, a typical oral dose is 250 mg four times daily (up to 2,000 mg/day). Phosphate replacement is dosed in mmol of phosphate according to the severity of hypophosphatemia, with IV regimens commonly 0.08-0.6 mmol/kg depending on serum level and dose reduction in renal dysfunction. The most important safety concern is with ORAL SODIUM PHOSPHATE BOWEL PREPARATIONS: the FDA added a boxed warning (December 2008) for rare but serious acute phosphate nephropathy (acute kidney injury, sometimes irreversible), and Fleet Phospho-soda OTC products were voluntarily withdrawn. Sources include BNF/Martindale-type monographs and FDA-labeled sodium phosphate products.
indications: Urinary acidification (to lower urine pH; adjunct in managing certain urinary stones, urinary odor, or to optimize action of some urinary anti-infectives)
Treatment and prevention of hypophosphatemia / phosphorus depletion (phosphate replacement)
Phosphorus supplementation in parenteral nutrition and selected metabolic conditions
Bowel cleansing before colonoscopy or other procedures (oral sodium phosphate prep - prescription only, with restrictions due to nephropathy risk)

dosage.d: 250 mg four times daily; may increase to 250 mg every 2 hours if urine is difficult to acidify
dosage.n: Maximum 2,000 mg/day; titrate to urine pH

dosage.d: Approximately 0.16-0.2 mmol/kg phosphate infused over ~6 hours
dosage.n: Reduce dose by 50% in renal impairment; recheck phosphorus

dosage.d: Approximately 0.5-0.6 mmol/kg phosphate over ~6 hours (intermediate ~0.4 mmol/kg for serum P 1.0-1.7 mg/dL)
dosage.n: Monitor closely; reduce 50% in renal dysfunction; avoid co-precipitation with calcium

dosage.d: Approximately 20-40 mmol phosphate per day, adjusted to serum levels
Per specific product labeling (e.g., OsmoPrep sodium phosphate tablet regimen)
dosage.n: Prescription only; observe FDA boxed warning and hydration requirements

admin: Take oral phosphate/acidifier with a full glass of water and with or after food to limit GI upset and diarrhea
For IV phosphate, dilute and infuse slowly (typically over several hours); do not bolus - risk of hypocalcemia, arrhythmia, and calcium-phosphate precipitation
Do not co-infuse phosphate with calcium-containing solutions in the same line (precipitation risk)
For oral bowel preps, ensure adequate hydration before, during, and after; screen for renal impairment and risk factors for phosphate nephropathy
Titrate urinary-acidifier dose to measured urine pH
moa: Sodium acid phosphate is the monobasic (acidic) sodium salt of phosphoric acid. As a urinary acidifier, the dihydrogen phosphate ion is excreted in urine and lowers urinary pH. As a phosphate source, it supplies inorganic phosphate needed for ATP, 2,3-DPG, bone mineralization, and acid-base buffering, correcting hypophosphatemia. In saline laxative and bowel-prep forms, the poorly absorbed phosphate salts act osmotically to draw water into the intestinal lumen, increasing intraluminal volume and promoting evacuation; this same osmotic shift and phosphate absorption underlie the fluid/electrolyte and renal risks of the oral bowel-prep products.

absolute: Severe renal impairment / acute kidney injury (for phosphate loading and oral bowel preps)
Hypocalcemia (uncorrected) - phosphate can further lower calcium
Known bowel obstruction, perforation, ileus, or toxic megacolon (for laxative/bowel-prep use)
relative: Heart failure, hypertension, or sodium-restricted states (sodium load)
Older age (>55 yr), hypovolemia, baseline kidney disease, or drugs affecting renal perfusion (increased acute phosphate nephropathy risk with oral preps)
monitor: Serum phosphorus, calcium, sodium, and potassium
Renal function (creatinine, eGFR) and hydration status
Urine pH when used as an acidifier

preg: Phosphate salts are generally considered low risk when used appropriately to correct deficiency or for short-term laxative use; maintain hydration and electrolyte balance. Use the lowest effective dose and monitor electrolytes.
lact: Phosphate is a normal milk and dietary constituent; appropriate therapeutic use is generally considered compatible with breastfeeding. Monitor maternal electrolytes if used in higher doses.
renal: Use with caution and reduce dose in renal impairment. Reduced phosphate clearance increases the risk of hyperphosphatemia, secondary hypocalcemia, and metastatic calcification; IV replacement doses are typically reduced by about 50%. Oral sodium phosphate bowel preps should generally be avoided in significant renal impairment because of the risk of acute phosphate nephropathy.
hepatic: No specific dose adjustment is required for hepatic impairment, but monitor fluid and electrolyte status, particularly in cirrhosis with fluid overload.

major: Other phosphate-containing products - additive hyperphosphatemia risk
Nephrotoxic drugs / agents reducing renal perfusion (NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, diuretics) with oral sodium phosphate bowel preps - increased acute phosphate nephropathy risk
moderate: Calcium and vitamin D / active vitamin D analogs - risk of calcium-phosphate precipitation and altered calcium balance
Antacids or sucralfate containing aluminum/magnesium/calcium - bind phosphate and reduce its absorption
Potassium-sparing or potassium supplements when potassium phosphate forms are used - hyperkalemia risk
minor: Urinary acidification may alter renal elimination of pH-dependent drugs (e.g., enhances excretion of weakly basic drugs)
interactions.food: Aluminum/magnesium/calcium-containing foods and antacids reduce phosphate absorption; take with water and food to limit GI upset.
interactions.alcohol: No direct interaction; alcohol can worsen dehydration, which is hazardous with bowel-prep use.
interactions.diagnostics: Can alter serum phosphate, calcium, and urine pH measurements; account for dosing timing when interpreting electrolytes.

common: Gastrointestinal upset: nausea, abdominal cramping, diarrhea (especially with oral/laxative use)
serious: Hyperphosphatemia with secondary hypocalcemia (tetany, paresthesia, arrhythmia) - especially with rapid IV or in renal impairment
Acute phosphate nephropathy / acute kidney injury with oral sodium phosphate bowel preps (may be irreversible, can require dialysis)
Fluid and electrolyte disturbances (hypernatremia, dehydration, hypokalemia) with bowel preps
rare: Cardiac arrhythmias related to electrolyte shifts
emergency: Acute kidney injury / oliguria after bowel prep

monitoring: Serum phosphorus, calcium, sodium, and potassium (baseline and during therapy)
Renal function (creatinine, eGFR) and hydration status, especially with bowel preps and in at-risk patients
Urine pH when used as a urinary acidifier
Cardiac/ECG monitoring with IV phosphate or significant electrolyte shifts
Signs of hypocalcemia (tetany, paresthesias) and fluid overload
counsel: Take oral doses with a full glass of water and with food to reduce stomach upset and diarrhea
Drink plenty of fluids - dehydration is dangerous, especially with bowel-prep products
If using a sodium phosphate bowel prep, follow hydration instructions exactly and tell your doctor about kidney disease, heart failure, or medicines like water pills, blood-pressure pills, or NSAIDs
Report muscle cramps, tingling, irregular heartbeat, reduced urination, or swelling
Do not exceed the recommended dose; for urinary acidification your doctor may check your urine pH
pk: Saline laxative effect within ~30 minutes to a few hours orally; IV phosphate corrects levels over hours
Variable; phosphate absorption and serum changes occur over hours
Phosphate is a physiologic ion regulated by kidney, parathyroid, and bone rather than a fixed drug half-life
Depends on dose and renal handling; acidifier effect persists while dosing continues
Store at room temperature; protect from freezing (solutions); follow product labeling
pearls: FDA BOXED WARNING / SAFETY ALERT: Oral sodium phosphate bowel preps (e.g., Visicol, OsmoPrep) carry a boxed warning (December 2008) for rare but serious ACUTE PHOSPHATE NEPHROPATHY (acute kidney injury, sometimes irreversible); OTC Fleet Phospho-soda products were voluntarily withdrawn
Highest nephropathy risk: age >55, hypovolemia/dehydration, baseline kidney disease, bowel obstruction/active colitis, and drugs affecting renal perfusion (diuretics, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, NSAIDs)
Urinary acidifier dose: 250 mg four times daily, up to 2,000 mg/day - titrate to urine pH
IV phosphate must be given slowly and never bolused; avoid co-administration with calcium (precipitation) and reduce dose ~50% in renal impairment
Regulatory note: FDA-labeled sodium phosphate injection and oral products exist; broader dosing/use references are based on BNF/Martindale-type monographs and FDA labeling
missed: For scheduled phosphate replacement or urinary acidification, take a missed oral dose when remembered unless it is near the next dose, then skip it - do not double up. For a one-time bowel prep, follow the specific timing in the product instructions or contact the prescriber rather than improvising.
overdose: Overdose can cause hyperphosphatemia with secondary hypocalcemia (tetany, paresthesias, arrhythmias), hypernatremia, dehydration, and acute kidney injury. Management is supportive: stop the product, rehydrate, correct calcium and other electrolytes, and monitor renal and cardiac function; dialysis may be needed in severe hyperphosphatemia or renal failure. Contact a poison control center (1-800-222-1222 in the U.S.) for guidance.
